narrative:
The model predicted a 63.4% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Placing in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) is substantially lower than the average of roughly 6 among students who were accepted. Your first-year ranking was the second most important factor and also increased the likelihood of failure; you ranked in the second decile compared with an average around 6 for admitted students. These two early indicators of academic performance outweighed everything else in the model’s eyes.

Your family income bracket worked in the opposite direction. Being from an upper-middle income family slightly lowered the predicted risk of failure, which aligns with the fact that most accepted students (45%) also come from this bracket. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the impact of your class rankings.

Your LSAT score of 28.5 and undergraduate GPA of 2.6 were also below the averages of accepted students (37.2 and 3.23 respectively), but they played a smaller role than your law-school performance.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record if you retake courses or apply again later. Consider targeted bar-prep programs that address gaps shown by your early class standings, and explore schools with more flexible admission criteria. Rebuilding a stronger transcript will be the most direct way to change future predictions in your favor. (248 words)
